en: Whimpering like a young puppy,
I, poor soul, am to die unshriven.
Without funeral prayer, without confession of faith,
I, poor soul, am to die unshriven.
Without even a crow to caw,
I am to die on the plain.
With my death thus upon me,
I am to die at my child's hands!
My river through the valley, my spring,
My orphan whom I saw after death,
My soft, pale-mottled falcon,
My gray goshawk, my morning star,
He has not yet learned to put on his shirt,
Does not know that I, poor soul, am his mother.
My scimitar left by the sword,
My lamp left by the precious one,
My hoof left by the wondrous steed,
My lamp left by the noble falcon,
My pennant fastened to the spear,
My gift left by the magnanimous one,
The ten companions gone to the next world—
He does not yet know it was their blessing,
The fierce warrior of saintly birth—
He does not yet know he was his father.
That I, poor soul, like a hunting hound
Ran, he does not yet know.
Fleeing Talas for the child's sake,
I came—he does not yet know.
Before the Five Wild Sheep stars set,
Five times returning to my breast,
He suckled—he does not yet know.
Crying out across Kuyuktun-Bel,
I crossed—he does not yet know.
Carrying him upon my back from Talas,
I fled—he does not yet know.
"A crazed unbeliever," he says,
"A woman running wild," he says,
"Dressed in men's clothes,
An abandoned unbeliever," he says.
It is your mother, I, you wretched soul!
If I show him my breast,
The orphan will never prosper, alas.
Today the bastard will not spare my life, alas.
"A raging unbeliever," he says,
And will seize me on my road, alas.
Today he will gouge my eyes, alas,
Not hear my words when I implore him.
He will seize me on my road, alas,
"A wretched woman," he says,
And drag me upon the road.
Today he will slaughter me in sacrifice, alas,
Making me cry out,
Gouging out my eyes,
Dragging me upon the road,
He will have dogs tear me apart, alas.
My bones will lie exposed upon the plain,
Will remain unburied, alas.
My dear hair like strands of silk,
Croaking ravens will tear, alas.
My dear eyes like a camel-calf's,
Black crows will peck out, alas.
Upon my mighty teeth as broad as doors,
Chattering magpies will shit today, alas.
My two breasts like apples,
Black vultures will peck, alas.
Wild with racing horses,
I, the woman overwhelmed by misfortune,
Will become a vulture's shit today, alas.
My quivering kidneys,
The wretched foxes will tear out, alas,
The flesh about my haunches,
Wolves will tear and eat their fill, alas.
Crows will tear my belly, alas.
When my backbone lies protruding,
The cursed crows will shit upon it, alas.
Boasting, such great prizes—
Why did I not refrain from seeking them?
I, a woman born for torment,
Mountain-like Taitoru—
Why did I not refrain from racing him!?
Alas, my brow bone was sloping;
After my king passed away,
My share of life was scant.
In the marshes of broad Talas,
When my sultan lay gravely ill,
When I turned my neck toward the Truth,
Coughing harshly again and again,
My fierce warrior raised his head from the pillow,
When he was in a dreadful state,
As a sacrifice, I, a wretched woman,
Why did I not die?
Smoothing his fine mustache,
My fierce warrior drew his life toward Judgment,
When he lay gravely ill,
As a sacrifice to the sultan,
Why did I not die!
Crying out in tears, unable to stand,
Why did I not become a snowcock?
Dying without hesitation,
For the sultan gone to the next world,
Why did I not become a sacrifice!
Unable to cross Chakmak-Bel,
Exhausted, weeping, unable to walk,
Blood running from my calves,
Strength leaving my wretched life,
What the Maker had drawn—
Why did I not face it?
Rather than outlive the fierce warrior,
Why did I not die?
The cradle upon my back—
Why did I not refrain from loading it?
So much of this hardship,
Tempted by this five-day life,
Why did I not refrain from bearing it!
With my thoughts torn apart,
Shameless soul, I am to die, alas,
By the child born of myself.
I have no support to lean upon,
No stronghold where I can take shelter.
When I suffer such cruel torment,
"My brave sister-in-law, do not weep,"
To comfort me with those words,
There are no valiant Kyrgyz here.
There is no cliff the goose cannot circle,
No black mountain with a ledge for me.
I have no way not to grieve.
“I was once a great man;
"My noble sister-in-law, stop," they would say,
And speak their words of counsel—
Are the Argyn and Kyrgyz here?
The line that Allah wrote
Is thus: let me face it.
Six times the telescope
Let me hold steady and extend.
If my bay horse does not come in all six,
If God will not grant it,
For six calves and forty yearlings
I bought Aktinte.
Let me draw it from its sheath,
Plunge it beneath my lower ribs,
Let me cut myself open.
Before I die at my son's hands,
Let me die by my own!
If he does not come in six looks,
If my wish is not granted,
Let me see the face of the next world.
On the day that takes me, let me shed my blood.
Six times through the telescope,
Without impatience, I, the passionate woman,
Let me look with care.
If he does not come in six looks,
If my wish is not granted,
After that let me die.'
Then your mother, built like a warrior,
Turned Akborchuk's head.
Sobbing as she offered prayer,
To God whose command is mighty
She cried out in repentance.
Turning its wheel,
The telescope left by Manas
She put right to her eye.
Turning its screw,
Bursting into tears,
She turned her swift steed's head.
That spirited woman, built like a warrior,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykei
Stood looking through the telescope.
That unfortunate woman was bewildered,
Despairing of her borrowed life,
Unable to regain her composure,
Burning with terrible grief.
The slope of It-Torpu
Your sister-in-law caught sight of,
And at the sight she rejoiced greatly.
'For this grief-stricken head,
There must be a day when the Night of Power comes.
For this grieving, wretched head,
Today must be the day to see my only child!
God will grant my wish,
O Almighty, Bahauddin,
Today my Taitoru will come forward, will he not?!
For this head that never saw the sun,
There will be a time of sunshine.
For this head without fortune,
The dawn will break clear, will it not?!'
'God will quench my fire,
God will brighten my brow.
He will bind the hair at my nape,
My dear Taitoru,
Will wash away my widow's name, will he not?'
Crying out for joy,
Bursting into tears,
When she looked through the telescope,
Upon the ridge of It-Torpu,
Along Kezen-Kyr,
'When I count, Taitoru,
My swift steed is coming,
Behind sixty horses.
He has lowered his head to the ground,
My dear swift steed,
Has taken strides like a wild sheep.
He has lowered his neck to the ground,
Has taken immeasurable strides.
The wind cannot match his trot;
He has begun to run in full strength.
No beast can match his pace;
He has begun to run as never before.
When he slopes down the descent,
My dear swift steed,
His forelegs strike like a roe deer's.
When he pulls uphill,
His mane and tail spread wide.
When he reaches level plain,
His hooves drum upon the ground.
The black steel bit
Cracks in the creature's throat.
His maw opens wide,
White foam mixed with blood
Splashes upon his breast.
The black steel bit
Clatters against his throat.
His tail like strands of silk
Lashes against his flanks.'
Thus running, leaning forward,
His noble head like a deer's
Was wrapped in pitch-black dust.
'There is a night like the Night of Power;
There is a day to brighten my brow!
God will lift my sorrow,
Will still my grieving voice!
All my sorrow scattering,
My brow opening into brightness,
Among horses, the blaze-faced wondrous steeds—
Almambet and Chubak, their names paired—
Will surely turn their gaze toward me.
The heroes gone to the next world
Will come to aid the widow!
Upon a poor soul like me
The Almighty will turn his gaze.
The forty chiltens, Khydyr and Ilyas,
If they will it, the bay horse
They will all urge forward together!'
Saying these words then,
Your courageous sister-in-law Kanykei
Her dear currant-black eyes
Turned and wiped once more.
Crying out, 'Bahauddin,'
Sobbing, calling on the one God,
The king's great telescope
She took deftly in her hand,
Then put it to her eye.
Your sister-in-law looked again
And learned the horses' news.
At the spur of the yellow hills,
At the jutting mountain's headland,
Upon the ridge of Koruuchu,
